title: The mysterious disappearance of the American general revives the theories about UFOs: What is claimed about his connections
excerpt: The mysterious disappearance of the American general revives the theories about UFOs: What is claimed about his connections
content:
mystery

Express newspaper

07/10/2026 0:34

The disappearance of a retired US Air Force general has brought back attention to theories linking him to secret programs for UFOs and unidentified aerial phenomena.

William Neil McCasland, 68, disappeared from his home in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on February 27.

According to reports, his phone, body-worn devices, and prescription glasses were left at home.

More than seven months later, he is still considered missing.

McCasland has held senior positions in US military research and directed the Air Force Research Laboratory, an institution that manages billions of dollars in military science and technology projects.

Precisely because of these roles, his name has been mentioned for years in circles dealing with UFO theories, especially in connection with old claims about the remains of a crashed object in Roswell.

David Grusch's claims

The attention increased after former intelligence official David Grusch made new statements about McCasland.

Grusch, who in 2023 testified under oath that the US government had operated secret programs for decades to recover and analyze objects of non-human origin, claimed that McCasland had been involved in efforts to prepare the American public for possible revelations about UFOs.

Speaking on Joe Rogan's podcast, Grusch linked this to Hillary Clinton's statements during the 2016 presidential campaign, when she had promised more transparency about the UFO files.

He also called it "very strange" that McCasland disappeared just days after Donald Trump announced on February 19 that he intended to release documents related to UFOs and extraterrestrials.

However, there is no public evidence that McCasland's disappearance is related to this announcement.

His name also appeared in WikiLeaks emails.

McCasland had held important positions at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Ohio and Kirtland Air Force Base in New Mexico.

His name also gained public attention in 2016, after WikiLeaks published hacked emails from John Podesta's account.

One of the messages, titled "General McCasland," described contacts between former Blink-182 member Tom DeLonge and the retired general.

DeLonge, who later became one of the most well-known public figures in the UAP field through the organization To The Stars Academy, wrote that he had worked with McCasland for several months.

According to the email, he claimed that the general not only understood his project, but had also helped him form a team of advisors.

In the same message, DeLonge also repeated the long-standing claim that material from the Roswell incident was sent to Wright-Patterson.

But the email offered no concrete evidence to support this claim.

Podesta disputes Grusch's interpretation

Grusch said that John Podesta had approved some kind of “public fit activity” and that that was why DeLonge had taken on certain advisors, including contacts with McCasland.

Podesta, however, disagrees with this description.

In an email response to PARADIGM, he said he would not characterize their interaction that way.

According to Podesta, the discussions were about declassifying Department of Defense documents and reducing the stigma against professionals who took UAP phenomena seriously.

He stressed that he had always believed that the American public was capable of handling the truth and that there was no need for an "adjustment" process.

Why DeLonge?

Grusch claimed that McCasland communicated with DeLonge because he could be used as a public figure with influence on young people.

According to him, the idea was to prepare the public ground before 2016.

This too remains Grusch's claim and has not been confirmed by public documents.

His wife doesn't believe there was a crime.

McCasland's wife, Susan Wilkerson, told local authorities in February that she did not believe her husband's disappearance was connected to any criminal act.

However, she told emergency operators that it appeared as if he "planned not to be found."

Local police have not reported any new public developments in this case.

Previous allegations of secret programs

David Grusch had previously claimed that McCasland was one of the officers who had responsibility for classified programs related to the recovery and analysis of non-human artifacts.

He also claimed that McCasland had not been cooperative with lawmakers seeking to interview people with knowledge of alleged U.S. contacts with extraterrestrial technology.

These claims have not been publicly substantiated by independent evidence.

For now, the disappearance of William Neil McCasland remains an open case, while his alleged links to secret UFO programs continue to fuel speculation that has not been officially confirmed. /GazetaExpress/
